title: FTC rulemaking after National Petroleum: statutory confirmation and constraints
shortTitle: FTC rulemaking after National Petroleum: statutory confirmation and constraints
summary: The Magnuson–Moss Act expressly addressed unfair-or-deceptive-practice rules while adding procedures; the text separately presents the FTC’s contested later theory for competition rules.
notes:
The 1975 Magnuson–Moss legislation confirmed FTC authority to adopt legislative rules concerning unfair or deceptive acts or practices and allowed civil-penalty enforcement of such rules. It also imposed additional procedures, including specified oral participation and opportunities to address disputed material facts. The reading’s historical account describes delays, organizational difficulties, litigation, and political resistance that followed, showing how broader formal authority can coexist with burdens on its exercise.

The assigned discussion distinguishes this consumer-protection authority from rules addressing unfair methods of competition. It reproduces the FTC’s 2024 noncompete-rule preamble, which argues that the 1975 and 1980 enactments preserved and ratified competition-rule authority under § 6(g). The argument points to savings language, deliberate legislative choices, and later analytical duties premised on substantive rules. Those are the Commission’s legal arguments as reproduced by the textbook. The editors expressly describe their interpretation as contested and explain why an agency might seek more specific statutory support than National Petroleum alone supplies.
